intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PAK2 gene (605022) on chromosome 3q29.

checks.claim: Knobloch syndrome-2 (KNO2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PAK2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We conclude that the KNO2 syndrome in the studied family is dominant and caused by a deleterious variant in the PAK2 gene.
checks.explanation: The abstract calls the variant monoallelic, which means heterozygous.

checks.claim: The PAK2 gene is located on chromosome 3q29.
checks.evidence_quote: Dominant monoallelic variant in the PAK2 gene causes Knobloch syndrome type 2.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is not in the abstract, but it is standard gene nomenclature that only restates the gene the paper names.

paragraphs.text: Knobloch syndrome is a disorder with high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration with retinal detachment, and congenital encephalocele (Menzel et al., 2004). In the family with Knobloch syndrome-2, the affected sibs also had intellectual disability and autistic behavior. Antonarakis et al. (2021) concluded that KNO2 is a dominant disorder in that family, unlike the autosomal recessive COL18A1-related form of Knobloch syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Wilson et al. (1998) reported 2 sibs with Knobloch syndrome. Both had high myopia, vitreoretinal degeneration, and either an occipital encephalocele or a scalp lesion. One sib had very early onset of severe eye disease. The other sib had only a very mild scalp defect. Both sibs also appeared to have an unusual pulmonary lymphatic condition.

paragraphs.text: Menzel et al. (2004) studied a Knobloch syndrome family from New Zealand and excluded linkage to the COL18A1 locus on chromosome 21q22.3. They took this as evidence for a second Knobloch syndrome locus, which they named KNO2.

paragraphs.text: Antonarakis et al. (2021) performed whole-exome sequencing on the 2 affected sibs of the KNO2 family and their unaffected parents. Both sibs carried a heterozygous missense mutation in the PAK2 gene, glu435-to-lys (E435K). The mutation was apparently de novo in both sibs, which suggested germline mosaicism in one parent. However, deep sequencing of the parents' blood DNA did not detect mosaicism. The mutation lies in the kinase domain, and structural analysis predicted that it might compromise kinase activity. In transfected HEK293T cells, the E435K mutation caused a partial loss of kinase activity.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with Knobloch syndrome-2 born to unaffected parents, Antonarakis et al. (2021) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a heterozygous glu435-to-lys (E435K) mutation in the kinase domain of the PAK2 gene. The mutation was apparently de novo in both sibs, which suggested parental germline mosaicism. However, deep sequencing of the parents' blood DNA did not detect mosaicism. Structural analysis predicted that the mutation might compromise kinase activity. In transfected HEK293T cells, the mutation caused a partial loss of kinase activity.
